transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Lena Cho (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Tess Nguyen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Orion CTO), Daniel Kim (Orion ML), Sara Thompson (Orion DevOps), Oliver Grant (advisor)

[00:00] Lena Cho: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, we'll do technical deep dive on the 128k long-context requirement and performance tradeoffs. Marco and Tess will lead the runtime/benchmark discussion.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Thanks, Lena. Real quick, our primary goal is to process patient records and genomic reports up to ~120-150k tokens. Latency targets are pretty tight for some UIs — around 2-4s for summary use cases, but batch jobs can be higher.
[00:34] Marco Ruiz: Got it. That's helpful. Just to confirm, those 2-4s are single-request tail latencies? or interactive where we can stream?
[00:48] Priya Nair: Interactive. Ideally first-pass summary in <4s for a 128k context. We realize that's aggressive.
[00:58] Daniel Kim: We can tolerate slower for heavy analytics, but for our clinician-facing interface low latency is needed.
[01:10] Tess Nguyen: Cool. We'll walk through server runtime strategies: KV caching, chunking (sliding-window + retrieval), attention optimizations like sparse attention / local-window + global tokens, and quantization impacts on both throughput and quality.
[01:29] Sara Thompson: Also want to confirm data path — we're leaning VPC private deployment. Compliance reasons, SOC2 plus local PII controls.
[01:39] Lena Cho: Noted. We'll cover VPC and on-prem considerations and what artifacts we'll need.

[05:12] Marco Ruiz: High-level approach for 128k: we rarely feed a full 128k monolithically. Two common patterns: 1) chunk+retrieve: split document into smaller chunks (4k-16k) with an index and retrieve a relevancy subset before generation; 2) long-kv caching: stream tokens into a KV cache and only run attention on the active window, exploiting efficient KV read paths. Each has tradeoffs.
[05:44] Priya Nair: We currently tried naive chunking but got hallucinations because context fragments lose global cohesion.
[05:53] Marco Ruiz: Yeah, that happens. You can mitigate via hierarchical prompts — e.g., precompute chunk-level summaries, then feed summaries plus relevant chunks. Another is overlap-sliding windows with redundancy to preserve context across window boundaries.
[06:12] Daniel Kim: For overlapping windows, how do you manage cost and latency blowup? Doubling tokens doubles cost and can blow latency.
[06:23] Tess Nguyen: Exactly. That's where intelligent retrieval + lightweight prefiltering helps. Also Redwood's runtime can pin quantized kernels for local attention windows which reduces per-token compute. The idea: only full self-attention on condensed representation, local windows and global tokens otherwise.

[09:05] Marco Ruiz: Let's talk numbers. For a 70B-class model on an A100-like instance, full attention on 128k context is extremely expensive — naive O(n^2) attention won't work. Our optimized runtime uses attention tiling and KV cache streaming; effective throughput for 128k workloads depends on quantization and attention scheme. In our internal 128k benchmarks, with 8-bit quantization and hybrid local+global attention we see median token latency reductions ~3x vs fp16 baseline for generation, and end-to-end summary latencies in the 2-6s range for tuned pipelines.
[09:45] Priya Nair: 2-6s range is promising. Can you share the benchmark spreadsheet?
[09:52] Lena Cho: Yes — will share after the call (link in next steps).

[12:10] Daniel Kim: On quantization: we're worried about QA/accuracy regressions. Which quant profiles do you recommend for long-context accuracy-sensitive tasks?
[12:22] Marco Ruiz: For tasks requiring high fidelity we recommend mixed approach: keep attention & final layers in higher precision (fp16) or use 4-bit with per-channel scales (GPTQ-style), keep embedding & norm layers higher precision. For long-context, preserving KV precision is critical — quantizing KV aggressively can degrade retrieval of far-history tokens. So we often quantize feedforward weights more aggressively than KV matrices.
[12:52] Priya Nair: Right, because KV stores the history.
[12:56] Tess Nguyen: One note: we can apply custom quantization for the KV path (8-bit) while using 4-bit for MLP to balance memory and quality. We'll include recommended autotune knobs in the artifact.

[15:30] Oliver Grant: How about hardware? We have access to on-prem H100 racks and cloud GPUs. Any preference?
[15:40] Marco Ruiz: H100 is great for throughput and optimized kernels for long-context attention. The kernel selection step in our runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution; H100 tends to win for 128k sliding-window throughput. But H100 memory layout and multi-GPU NVLink topology matter for KV partitioning.
[15:59] Sara Thompson: If we do VPC deployment, how much control over NVLink / topology do we get? We're on AWS with Nitro instances currently — we'd prefer a provider-managed dedicated metal or on-prem for tight topology.
[16:15] Tess Nguyen: For Redwood Private in a VPC, we can operate in your cloud VPC with dedicated instances. For true NVLink topologies you may need dedicated metal / on-prem or cloud bare metal procurement. We'll run a sizing exercise.

[19:02] Marco Ruiz: Let's dig into KV cache strategies. For 128k, you want to avoid re-attending to the full context each generation step. We stream KV blocks and maintain a multi-level cache: recent active window (dense, fast access), large cold store (sharded, compressed). Access patterns: most queries hit recent window; for rare far-history access we issue a retrieval into the active window.
[19:34] Daniel Kim: That implies a retrieval layer — we'll need fast indexing. What are typical chunk sizes and index strategies?
[19:44] Marco Ruiz: Usually 2k-8k chunk sizes for semantic vectors; you can do 16k for chunked compressed segments. Indexing uses approximate nearest neighbors (FAISS/HNSW) with metadata to rapidly filter by doc id + timestamp. We also keep precomputed chunk-level summaries to reduce number of chunks pulled into the active window.

[22:05] Priya Nair: Can Redwood's runtime operate with our existing retrieval system? We run an internal vector DB.
[22:14] Tess Nguyen: Yes — runtime has adapters for external vector DBs. We can integrate with your HNSW/FAISS cluster; we recommend a lightweight sidecar to handle chunk-to-KV translation and prefetching.

[25:30] Marco Ruiz: On attention optimizations: two big classes — structured sparsity (local windows + global tokens) and low-rank / Linformer approximations. For many doc understanding tasks, local-window attention plus a small set of global summary tokens gives a nearly linear scaling while preserving cross-chunk reasoning. We also support attention caching kernels that stream KV blocks and only compute attention for non-cached parts.
[26:02] Daniel Kim: Does Redwood support sliding window attention with overlap? How do you prevent double-counting?
[26:12] Marco Ruiz: Yes. Overlap is a tuning knob. To avoid double-counting you can apply chunk-level gating or use composite prompts that mark token offsets and use position-aware retrieval so the model understands chunk boundaries. There's also a strategy to generate chunk summaries first and then aggregate, which reduces duplication.

[29:40] Priya Nair: On the security side, for VPC/on-prem, what's the onboarding for KMS/HSM and audit logs?
[29:51] Tess Nguyen: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and can support HSM. Audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM (Splunk, Datadog) or retained in your object storage. We'll provide SOC2 artifacts and a security architecture diagram.

[32:05] Sara Thompson: How invasive is the software on our infra? We need the ability to air-gap.
[32:15] Marco Ruiz: We have an on-prem package that can be air-gapped. It requires a small control-plane node initially for licensing and then can operate fully offline; updates are done via signed bundles. We'll share the on-prem checklist.

[35:00] Marco Ruiz: Back to benchmarks — we'll recommend a two-phase benchmark: 1) synthetic microbenchmarks for pure kernel/token throughput (measure token/s, memory, and tail latencies), 2) end-to-end pipeline benchmarks using your sample dataset with retrieval + chunking to measure user-visible latency and quality. We'll provide a spreadsheet template and a latency trace format.
[35:34] Daniel Kim: For microbenchmarks, what's the recommended sampler? We want p99/p999 numbers.
[35:41] Marco Ruiz: We recommend real-time traffic replication and a synthetic harness that replays request arrival patterns; for p99/p999 we collect per-token and per-request histograms and export to Prometheus/OTel. We'll include a Jupyter with the analysis scripts.

[38:20] Priya Nair: On cost — if we go H100 on-prem vs cloud H100, what's the delta? Rough numbers are fine now.
[38:30] Lena Cho: In general, on-prem capex amortized can be cheaper at scale, cloud is Opex but with flexibility. For 128k workloads you need more memory/sharding so instance count increases; we'll include a cost model in the spreadsheet comparing dedicated H100 racks vs cloud instances.

[41:58] Oliver Grant: A question on model variants — can you fall back to smaller models for retrieval-only tasks?
[42:06] Tess Nguyen: Yes, smart routing can send cheap retrieval-only requests to lightweight embedder/encoder models and only invoke the big model for final generation. This saves cost and keeps latencies low for many queries.

[44:12] Daniel Kim: Any gotchas with quantization + mixed precision across multi-gpu setups? We had instabilities when combining 4-bit GPTQ with model parallelism.
[44:24] Marco Ruiz: That happens. Mixing quantization with tensor/model parallelism requires careful kernel selection and consistent quant scales across shards. Our runtime performs a calibration pass and will fall back to per-GPU fp16 for certain critical ops if calibration fails. We also log quality regressions and auto-tune.

[47:55] Priya Nair: For the UI use case we talked about, do you think we should aim to precompute summaries nightly and use retrieval for live micro-summary updates?
[48:07] Marco Ruiz: That's reasonable: precompute heavy summaries offline and keep a live delta for recent changes. Many customers use hybrid offline+online pipelines to hit strict latencies.

[50:21] Sara Thompson: Regarding network — how much bandwidth do we need for KV streaming across NVLink vs ethernet?
[50:32] Marco Ruiz: NVLink has far higher effective bandwidth and lower latency — for KV streaming at 128k you want NVLink for multi-GPU nodes to avoid cross-host network penalties. Over ethernet we recommend compressing KV blocks and prefetching aggressively and expect higher latencies. We'll include network-sizing guidance in the artifact.

[52:10] Tess Nguyen: Quick demo note — we can run a 128k pilot on your sample dataset. It typically takes 2-4 weeks to run benchmarking and tuning, depending on dataset sanitization and infra access.
[52:22] Priya Nair: Good. We'll prioritize the dataset and infra notes.

[55:00] Marco Ruiz: A few more practicality points: 1) use position-aware chunk IDs so you can reconstruct spans; 2) tune overlap and summary length iteratively; 3) monitor perplexity drift as you change quantization — small drift can be acceptable but watch for hallucinations.

[58:15] Daniel Kim: On monitoring — what observability do you provide at token-level and route-level?
[58:25] Lena Cho: Redwood Console has token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and sampling of model outputs. We can ship traces to your APM and provide alerting for regression in quality metrics tied to eval prompt sets.

[61:40] Priya Nair: Any final notes on privacy for long context — storing KV means keeping history. How do we manage TTL and revocation?
[61:50] Tess Nguyen: We support configurable retention policies and encryption-at-rest for KV stores. For revocation we can purge KV shards and rotate keys, but note that key rotation strategies must be coordinated with the runtime to avoid inability to read old KVs. We'll include recommended key-rotation playbook.

[65:05] Lena Cho: Alright, quick recap actions: we'll share benchmark spreadsheet, Marco will produce quantization and chunking recommendations, Tess will schedule the VPC/on-prem workshop, and Orion will provide datasets and infra notes.
[65:25] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Appreciate the depth.
[65:33] Daniel Kim: One last question — any reference docs for long-context attention kernels?
[65:40] Marco Ruiz: We'll share internal notes and a pointer to the runtime kernel guide (docs link).
[66:00] Lena Cho: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts and a calendar invite for the workshop.
[66:10] Meeting ended.
